title: Symmetric integral
problem: Evaluate \(\int_{-2}^{2} x^3 \cos(x^2)\, dx\). Check this solution — tap a step if it slips, or let it pass.
steps: Flipping the sign of \(x\) flips the sign of \(x^3 \cos(x^2)\), and \([-2, 2]\) is symmetric around \(0\).
So everything on \([-2, 0]\) cancels everything on \([0, 2]\).
Therefore \(\int_{-2}^{2} x^3 \cos(x^2)\, dx = 0\), without finding any antiderivative.
Not even a messy \(\sin 4\) or \(\cos 4\) survives at the endpoints.

meta.topic: Odd symmetry on a symmetric definite integral

explanation: Skipping the antiderivative sounds lazy, except \(x^3\) is odd and \(\cos(x^2)\) is even, so their product is strictly odd and cancels out over \([-2, 2]\).
